teaser: A tea party and a myth share the same beach, and Matisse is about to break the rules.
review_notes:
Identification of the clothed woman as Amélie Matisse and the wrapped child as their son Pierre: traditional reading.
Signac bought the painting in 1905 and hung it in the dining room of his villa La Hune in Saint-Tropez: standard account.
Painting remained with Signac's heirs until it entered French national collections (dation, 1982): please confirm date; lesson only says 'for decades'.
Raoul Dufy's reaction on seeing the painting in 1905 is paraphrased, not quoted.
Dimensions 98.5 x 118.5 cm.
Matisse painted the final canvas in Paris in the winter of 1904-05 from studies made in Saint-Tropez.

lesson.text: Something does not add up on this beach. On the left, a woman in a hat and a long dress sits by a tablecloth laid with teacups: a family picnic in 1904. A few steps away, naked women stretch, crouch and wring out their hair like nymphs from an ancient legend. Nobody seems to notice anybody else.

Henri Matisse built the picture on that clash. He spent the summer of 1904 in Saint-Tropez, then a quiet fishing village on the French Riviera, with his wife Amélie and their small son. The picnic is real life. The bathers come from somewhere else: a dream of a golden age that painters had been repeating for centuries.

lesson.title: Two worlds, one shore
lesson.text: Meet the picnic first, then the myth.

spots.title: The clothed woman
spots.text: Hat, dark dress, seated upright at the edge of the cloth. She is usually identified as Amélie Matisse. She is the only adult dressed for the twentieth century.

spots.title: The tea things
spots.text: Cups, saucers and a small pot on a pale cloth. An ordinary still life, the kind you would unpack from a basket.

spots.title: The bather
spots.text: A standing nude lifts her arms to twist her long hair, a pose straight out of old paintings of Venus rising from the sea. She belongs to no year at all.

lesson.text: The title tells you which world wins. It is a line from Charles Baudelaire's poem “Invitation to the Voyage,” which imagines a faraway land where everything is “luxury, calm and pleasure.” Matisse was not painting Saint-Tropez. He was painting the wish to be somewhere perfect, using Saint-Tropez as raw material.

Matisse came to painting late. He was a law clerk of twenty, stuck in bed after appendicitis, when his mother gave him a box of paints to pass the time. He later said it felt like being carried off to a kind of paradise.

Then there is the surface, which looks like a mosaic. His neighbor that summer was Paul Signac, the leading champion of Divisionism. The method: do not mix colors on the palette. Lay them side by side in small separate touches of pure paint, and let the viewer's eye do the mixing from a distance. In theory this made colors glow more brightly.

Matisse, 34 and still searching for a style, decided to try the system on a large canvas, nearly 1 by 1.2 m (about 39 by 47 in). He worked it up in Paris that winter from sketches. Before the brick-like strokes, he laid down a firm skeleton to hold the scene steady.
Under the confetti, the picture stands on a few straight beams.

lines.label: The horizon
lines.text: A band of blue and violet hills cuts the canvas a little above the middle. Above it, sky. Below it, everything that happens.

lines.label: The pine
lines.text: One tree trunk runs almost the full height at the right, like the edge of a stage. It stops your eye from sliding out of the picture.

lines.label: The mast
lines.text: The tilted mast of a beached boat leans across the center. It is the only strong diagonal, and it points from the bathers up into the blazing sky.

lines.label: The frieze
lines.text: The figures line up along the shore in a shallow chain, like carvings on a temple wall. Picnic and myth are stitched into one row.

lesson.text: With the structure settled, the color could go wild. Sand turns red and orange. Shadows turn blue and green. The sky runs from pink to lemon yellow. None of this is what a camera would have recorded on that beach. Matisse picks each color for what it does to its neighbors, not for what it copies.
In this painting color stops describing things and starts creating a feeling. The beach is hot because the paint is hot.
And yet Matisse was a restless pupil. Strict Divisionism forbids lines: forms should emerge from the dots alone. He could not resist. Zoom in on the bodies and you catch him cheating.
A small figure wrapped in a towel is standing among the bathers. Can you spot the child?

spots.title: The child
spots.text: Probably Matisse's young son Pierre, bundled up after a swim. See the blue and green contour that fences him in: a drawn line, exactly what Signac's method was supposed to do away with.

lesson.text: Those outlines were the future. Matisse found the dot system stiff, and felt that the little strokes fought with the drawing instead of serving it. The following summer, in the fishing port of Collioure, he dropped the method, kept the blazing color, and brushed it on in broad free patches. Critics called the result “Fauve,” wild beast.

Signac loved the painting. He bought it in 1905 and hung it in the dining room of his villa in Saint-Tropez, where it stayed in his family for decades. He was far less pleased with what Matisse painted next.

Shown in Paris in the spring of 1905, the canvas shook up younger painters. Raoul Dufy, then a follower of the Impressionists, said that standing in front of it changed his idea of what painting was for: imagination could now lead, and realism could follow or stay home.
Wander the surface for yourself. Notice how the strokes change size and direction from one zone to the next, and how much bare pale ground shows between them.

spots.title: The yellow sky
spots.text: Long horizontal dabs of lemon and pale pink, with a streak of orange cloud. The strokes lie flat, like the calm of late afternoon.

spots.title: The seated bather
spots.text: Knees drawn up, arm raised to her head, sitting on a red cloth. Her skin is built from pink, lilac and green touches, held together by an outline.

spots.title: The sleeper
spots.text: A nude lies back with her arms behind her red hair. Her body is the palest area on the sand, so it shines against the hot ground.

spots.title: The crouching figure
spots.text: Seen from behind, folded over, almost entirely in shadow colors: deep green, blue and yellow. A body treated as pure pattern.

spots.title: The boat
spots.text: A beached sailboat, its rigging drawn as dotted lines. Dashes stand in for ropes, a witty use of the dot method.

spots.title: Green against violet
spots.text: Sharp green leaves against a lilac trunk and blue water. Cool colors gather on this side to balance the hot reds on the left.

spots.title: The far shore
spots.text: The hills across the bay are plain bands of blue and mauve. Distance is made with cooler color, not with haze or detail.

lesson.text: The poem that gave the picture its name comes from Baudelaire's The Flowers of Evil, a book that was put on trial for offending public morals when it appeared in 1857.

So the contradiction on the beach was never settled, and that is its charm. A wife with her teacups, goddesses drying their hair, a borrowed technique and a painter already itching to abandon it: this is what a turning point looks like before anyone knows it is one.

quiz.question: Where does the painting's title come from?
quiz.explanation: It quotes a line from Baudelaire's “Invitation to the Voyage.”

quiz.question: What is the basic rule of Divisionism?
options: Paint only in black and white
Blend colors smoothly on the palette
Place small touches of pure color side by side
quiz.explanation: The colors are meant to mix in the viewer's eye, not on the palette.

quiz.question: Which painter was Matisse's neighbor in Saint-Tropez and later bought the picture?
quiz.explanation: Signac, the champion of Divisionism, bought it in 1905.

quiz.question: How does Matisse break the Divisionist rules here?
options: He draws contour lines around the figures
quiz.explanation: Colored outlines fence in the bodies, which the strict method avoided.

quiz.question: What did Matisse do the summer after this painting?
options: Kept the bright color but dropped the dots
quiz.explanation: At Collioure he used free patches of strong color, soon labeled Fauve.

facts.text: Every figure on the beach is nude.
facts.explanation: A clothed woman in a hat sits by the picnic, and a child is wrapped in a towel.

facts.text: Matisse started painting only around age twenty, while recovering from an illness.
facts.explanation: His mother gave him a paint box during his recovery from appendicitis.

facts.text: The colors match what Matisse actually saw on the beach.
facts.explanation: Red sand and blue shadows were chosen for their effect, not copied from nature.
